title: What's a brownfield remediation project?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain brownfield sites: abandoned or potentially contaminated industrial and commercial properties (old dry cleaners, gas stations) whose suspected contamination deters redevelopment. They contrast brownfields with Superfund sites, using Robins Air Force Base in Houston County, Georgia (sludge pond with Agent Orange, chemical waste, and unexploded ordnance covered with loam) as a Superfund example. They cover liability as an economic barrier, the estimate of roughly 450,000 brownfields in the US, Atlantic Station in Atlanta as a redevelopment example, government incentives including federal and state funding (Texas, Maine, Baltimore, Georgia's bill for 600 sites), tax increment financing, tax breaks, remediation methods (soil removal, bioremediation bacteria, phytoremediation with trees and plants, covering), the EPA's note that about one third of sites are contamination-free, and green brownfield remediation. The episode closes with listener mail from Shelby about a nightmare involving Disney.

segments.title: Opening banter and brownfield question
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode, joke around, and Josh begins answering 'what's a brownfield' with a definition.

segments.title: Brownfields versus Superfund sites
segments.summary: Josh defines a brownfield as a potentially contaminated abandoned site, distinguishing it from a Superfund site. He describes Robins Air Force Base in Georgia, where a sludge pond holding chemical waste, tires, unexploded ordnance and Agent Orange was covered with loam.

segments.title: Economic liability and reuse benefits
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how suspected contamination and liability keep developers away from brownfields, and how reusing these sites spares greenfield land and existing infrastructure. They cite an estimate of about 450,000 brownfields in the United States.

segments.title: Government funding and incentives
segments.summary: The hosts describe federal and state brownfield funding, citing Texas, Maine, Baltimore and a Georgia bill to clean up 600 sites, and mention the Power Station in Baltimore as a remediated site.

segments.title: Tax increment financing and tax breaks
segments.summary: Chuck explains tax increment financing, where governments fund remediation based on projected tax revenue from increased property values, and notes tax breaks for cleanup costs.

segments.title: How brownfields are remediated
segments.summary: The hosts outline the process: site assessment and soil testing, the EPA's note that about one third of sites are clean, soil removal (with the Florence, South Carolina nuclear bomb debris moved to Savannah as an example), bioremediation bacteria, phytoremediation with trees, and covering.

segments.title: Green brownfield remediation
segments.summary: The hosts describe green brownfield remediation, using wind or solar power and alternative fuels for remediation equipment, as encouraged by the EPA.

segments.title: Listener mail: Shelby's Disney nightmare
segments.summary: A listener named Shelby writes about a vivid nightmare involving a Disney-led plot, which the hosts react to humorously before the closing sign-off.
